When the British left in 1947, about two fifths of India's land and a quarter of its people were not in British India at all. They lived in some 565 princely states, tied to the Crown by treaty. Within two years almost all were part of India or Pakistan.

British rule over the princes simply ended, leaving each free in law to join either country or neither. A patchwork of hundreds of states was a real danger. Vallabhbhai Patel and his civil servant V. P. Menon offered a simple deal: sign over defence, foreign affairs and communications, and keep your palace, title and a pension. The viceroy, Mountbatten, urged the princes to accept. By 15 August 1947 nearly all had.

Three held out:

  • Junagadh: its Muslim ruler chose Pakistan, though his people were mostly Hindu. Indian troops moved in, and a vote went for India.
  • Hyderabad: the Nizam, the richest prince, wanted independence. The Indian army took the state in five days in September 1948 (see Hyderabad State).
  • Kashmir: its Hindu ruler joined India in October 1947 when fighters from Pakistan invaded (see the Kashmir conflict).

The states were then merged into larger units and the princes lost all power. Their pensions were ended in 1971.
